title: Array indexing is 2-3x slower on 2024.12.0
body:

**Describe the issue**:

Array indexing can be 2-3x slower on `2024.12.0`, at least in certain cases when dealing with many chunks. I've narrowed it down to #11548 as the source of the change.

**Minimal Complete Verifiable Example**:

```python
import dask.array as da
import numpy as np

x = da.ones((1000000,), chunks=(1,))
%timeit x[np.arange(x.size)]
```

```
Before #11548
884 ms ± 29.5 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)

After
2.14 s ± 15.5 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Can you try this on the newest version?

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: I get 1.91s, so there must have been some other marginal improvements but still a significant regression.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Profile indicates this is all time creating the `Task` class in `take`:

![Image](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/ac35d77b-0257-472c-ba85-ed0728fccec0)

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Yeah, this was an intentional change. I don't know if there is much that we can do about the overhead of the constructor

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: why does slicing an array require creating a large number of objects?

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: This isn't really slicing, it's a positional indexer which could be out of order with a different indexer per chunk

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Probably a more realistic example:
```python
x = da.ones((100, 100000, 100000), chunks=(-1, 100, 100))
%timeit x[0, ...]
```

```
before:
1.78 s ± 123 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
after:
5.15 s ± 121 ms per loop (mean ± std. dev. of 7 runs, 1 loop each)
```

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: Thanks for the profiling. This isn't super surprising unfortunately and we have to keep track of the dependencies somewhere.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body: Yeah feel free to close if this is unavoidable. It's made basic subsetting of large zarr stores noticeably more sluggish so I wanted to at least document the issue.

comments.author: participant1
comments.body:
Yeah , I fully agree that the UX is worse through this. 

We are working on a more general solution that will defer the graph creation until you actually press compute, as a result your call above will be more or less instant. That *should* help with UX and just prolong the compute a little bit.

comments.author: participant2
comments.body: also, zarr itself should provide tools for subsetting zarr arrays, which would be nearly instant. I am extremely interested in adding this to zarr (but swamped with other stuff atm)

comments.author: participant1
comments.body: The change we are working on would also give us the option of pushing these slices directly into zarr, so that would be very appreciated as a feature in zarr itself

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
I just merged a PR that should help with performance a lot. 

The performance is not back to where it was for all cases but for most and a lot of the "worse performance" should be amortized by better runtime down the line.
If you are still experiencing issues, please reopen and provide a reproducer. Getting the reproducer right is important since there are a couple of different edge cases to consider.

comments.author: reporter
comments.body:
Thanks for the improvements!

Unfortunately the case where I originally noticed this is the one that #11945 doesn't do much for, which is ND with slicing.

Reproducer is something like this:
```python
x = da.ones((3000, 35, 720, 1440, 31), chunks=(1, -1, 72, 72, -1))
%timeit x[slice(None, -1), slice(None, 10)]
```

```
2024.11.2 -> 0.58s
2025.4.0 -> 1.75s
main -> 1.39s
```

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
I opened https://github.com/dask/dask/pull/11946 with another fix for this specific case. We're still not back to where we were but when looking at the end to end chain the performance either stays the same or improves.

I realize that there is a UX component to this but with the current code this is about as much as I can squeeze out

comments.author: participant3
comments.body:
Unfortunately, I had to revert one edge case that I thought was a noop but turns out isn't in https://github.com/dask/dask/pull/11947
However, as pointed out in https://github.com/dask/dask/pull/11946 the end-to-end runtime performance should generally be improved now even if the slicing itself is slower. Later stages during graph generation and scheduling are typically a bit faster now.
